Our evaluation covers three datasets but only one RE benchmark (SciERC), where 40\% of instances receive zero F1, compressing the discriminable range and limiting signal differentiation for relation extraction.
RE selection failure persists even when restricting to non-zero F1 instances (Appendix~\ref{app:re_conditional_selection}), ruling out floor effects as the sole explanation, but generalization to other RE benchmarks remains unvalidated.
WNUT-17 confirms the capability boundary of our approach, but our positive results on formal-domain text (CoNLL, SciERC) have not been validated on informal or noisy text where models achieve non-trivial performance.

We evaluate two model families (Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B), both at 8B parameters.
A 3-seed robustness analysis confirms that signal rankings are stable across seeds ($\sigma{\leq}0.026$; Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}), but whether our findings---particularly the correlation-selection gap and the difficulty-dependent signal ordering---hold for larger models (70B+) or closed-source APIs remains untested.
Larger models may produce higher-quality and more diverse samples, potentially altering the signal landscape.

Our analysis of selection potential uses only unsupervised signals.
We do not train a dedicated verifier or reward model, leaving unknown how much of the oracle headroom a supervised approach could recover.

We evaluate at $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$.
The behavior of confidence signals at larger sample sizes (e.g., $N{=}64$ or $N{=}128$) is unknown, and $N$-scaling gains are setting-dependent: SJ improves by $+0.047$ on Qwen SciERC NER but only $+0.016$ on LLaMA SciERC NER when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$.

On CoNLL with LLaMA, the SJ--FK gap is only 0.003 ($\rho{=}0.431$ vs.\ $0.428$), so the structural advantage over surface signals may not generalize to all simple-schema datasets.
Our free-form ablation (\S\ref{sec:ablation}) confirms that LP score compression persists without constrained decoding, but was conducted on a single dataset (SciERC) with one model (Qwen3-8B); whether the compression finding generalizes to other datasets, model families, or model scales remains untested.

Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint was trained with \texttt{enable\_thinking} active, injecting empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks (4--5 tokens, no reasoning chain) before each response; CoNLL and WNUT checkpoints disabled this feature.
At inference time, constrained decoding suppresses thinking tokens in all configurations, so they do not appear in generated samples.
The empty blocks may weakly affect first-token probability distributions during training, potentially shifting LP score calibration on SciERC; however, since LP selection fails across all datasets including CoNLL and WNUT-17 (which lack this confound), the thinking token inconsistency is unlikely to explain the correlation-selection gap.
The absence of any reasoning content further limits the representational impact.

One of three seeds (seed${=}456$) was run with \texttt{--subtask joint} (joint NER+RE decoding) rather than \texttt{--subtask ner} used by the other two seeds; the resulting NER F1 difference is ${<}0.3$~pp and falls within normal seed variance, so we retain this seed in 3-seed analyses without correction.

Finally, log-probability was excluded from the temperature comparison ($T{=}0.7$ vs.\ $T{=}1.0$) due to missing $T{=}0.7$ LP data; all LP compression analyses use $T{=}1.0$ exclusively, and whether compression behavior changes at lower temperatures remains unknown.
The free-form ablation (within-instance std ratio $0.97{\times}$) provides stronger evidence that compression is not an artifact of the decoding strategy, but does not address temperature as a variable.
Since practitioners commonly deploy at $T{<}1.0$ for reliability, this untested dependence represents a gap between our evaluation conditions ($T{=}1.0$) and typical deployment settings.
Lower temperatures concentrate probability mass on fewer tokens, which could either reduce LP compression (by widening score gaps between high- and low-probability sequences) or exacerbate it (by collapsing diversity so that all $N$ samples share near-identical token-level likelihoods).
The direction of this interaction is not predictable from first principles and depends on how the model's likelihood surface interacts with the structured output space.
Resolving this would require a controlled $T$-sweep with LP data at each temperature, which our experimental pipeline did not collect.

1	\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}
2	
3	\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}
4	For per-instance quality ranking, VC provides the strongest rank correlation ($\rho{=}0.38$), though EM leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.749$); under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$; RE: preliminary, single benchmark).
5	Signal rankings depend on task difficulty---EM dominates easy tasks (CoNLL), VC and SJ dominate hard tasks (SciERC)---directionally consistent across two model families at 8B scale, though with model-dependent magnitude.
6	At higher sample sizes ($N{=}16$), SJ converges to comparable NER performance with VC ($\Delta{=}0.002$) with lower cross-seed variance ($\sigma{=}0.010$ vs.\ $0.026$); on RE, only VC consistently outperforms LP (preliminary).
7	When model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17), all signals converge toward non-significant conditional correlations (Table~\ref{tab:wnut}).
8	
9	\paragraph{Why the gap exists: two layers.}
10	\textit{Layer 1 (definitional):} Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input; they cannot rank candidates by construction.
11	Consensus-proximity selection (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}) does not recover per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
12	\textit{Layer 2 (score compression):} Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails to exploit the 12--18~pp oracle headroom.
13	LP scores are severely compressed: the median within-instance LP range is only 0.041 nats, below the $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold at which 60\% of instances are effectively tied, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons fall within $|\Delta|{<}0.026$ (Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}).
14	In the 40\% of instances where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP \textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$; within-instance $\rho$: 0.08$\to$0.39).
15	This diagnostic confirms that LP carries useful per-sample quality information; score compression is the primary mechanistic bottleneck.
16	A controlled NER ablation (\S\ref{sec:ablation}) confirms that LP compression persists without constrained decoding; on RE, the interaction is task-dependent.
17	Diversity-stratified analysis confirms the gap persists even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}); RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339, preliminary; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}) may compound this.
18	
19	\paragraph{The gap widens with $N$.}
20	Doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$ expands oracle headroom from 12.5 to 16.9~pp ($+4.4$~pp), yet signal-based selection fails to capture this growth.
21	LP, the best signal, improves by only $+0.4$~pp ($\Delta$: $+0.0{\to}+0.5$~pp), leaving 16.4~pp of headroom unrealized---a 31\% expansion of the gap.
22	VC deteriorates further ($\Delta$: $-2.5{\to}{-}3.1$~pp), a counterintuitive result for majority voting: with more candidates, systematic errors in entity-level frequency counts dominate, amplifying selection bias rather than correcting it.
23	On RE at $N{=}16$ (3-seed), the pattern is even more severe: oracle headroom reaches 17.1~pp, yet all four consistency signals fall below greedy (best: VC $\Delta{=}{-}0.8$~pp; worst: EM $\Delta{=}{-}1.5$~pp; all Fisher $p{>}0.77$; Table~\ref{tab:re_n16_selection}).
24	LP is the sole exception ($\Delta{=}{+}0.7$~pp, Fisher $p{=}0.058$), the only positive selection delta on either task at $N{=}16$, but does not reach significance.
25	This scaling behavior confirms that the correlation-selection gap is not a small-$N$ artifact; unsupervised signals face a structural ceiling that widens as oracle headroom grows.
26	
27	\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
28	Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
29	Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here because the utility functions correlate with F1 at the instance level but not within a single instance---the mathematical essence of the correlation-selection gap.
30	\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs---consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.
31	
32	\paragraph{Score compression under free-form decoding.}\label{sec:ablation}
33	A natural hypothesis is that LP compression is an artifact of constrained decoding's restricted token space.
34	We test this via controlled ablation on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, single dataset): generating free-form (unconstrained) outputs on the same instances with post-hoc JSON parsing (parse rate 99.95\%, 4406/4408; Table~\ref{tab:freeform_ablation}).
35	For NER, LP variance is essentially unchanged (within-instance std ratio $0.97{\times}$, tied fraction 59.7\%$\to$57.7\%) and selection gains remain negligible ($+0.18$~pp free-form vs.\ $+0.59$~pp constrained), establishing that NER LP compression persists independent of decoding regime in our setting.
36	However, the ablation reveals a task-dependent interaction: RE LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single seed).
37	This reversal falls within the NER bootstrap 95\% CI [$-3.0$, $+4.2$]~pp and is based on a single seed, so we do not treat it as a confirmed finding; it suggests that constrained decoding may interact differently with RE but requires multi-seed replication.
38	The NER/RE divergence indicates that the relationship between decoding regime and selection is task-specific in our setting.
39	Notably, the fine-tuned model achieved 99.95\% parse rate without grammar constraints, suggesting that constrained decoding's format-compliance role may be redundant for sufficiently fine-tuned models.
40	
41	\paragraph{Task-specific decoding interactions.}
42	The free-form ablation reveals divergent behavior across tasks.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}
For per-instance quality ranking, VC provides the strongest rank correlation ($\rho{=}0.38$), though EM leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.749$); under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$; RE: preliminary, single benchmark).
Signal rankings depend on task difficulty---EM dominates easy tasks (CoNLL), VC and SJ dominate hard tasks (SciERC)---directionally consistent across two model families at 8B scale, though with model-dependent magnitude.
At higher sample sizes ($N{=}16$), SJ converges to comparable NER performance with VC ($\Delta{=}0.002$) with lower cross-seed variance ($\sigma{=}0.010$ vs.\ $0.026$); on RE, only VC consistently outperforms LP (preliminary).
When model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17), all signals converge toward non-significant conditional correlations (Table~\ref{tab:wnut}).

\paragraph{Why the gap exists: two layers.}
\textit{Layer 1 (definitional):} Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input; they cannot rank candidates by construction.
Consensus-proximity selection (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}) does not recover per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
\textit{Layer 2 (score compression):} Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails to exploit the 12--18~pp oracle headroom.
LP scores are severely compressed: the median within-instance LP range is only 0.041 nats, below the $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold at which 60\% of instances are effectively tied, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons fall within $|\Delta|{<}0.026$ (Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}).
In the 40\% of instances where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP \textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$; within-instance $\rho$: 0.08$\to$0.39).
This diagnostic confirms that LP carries useful per-sample quality information; score compression is the primary mechanistic bottleneck.
A controlled NER ablation (\S\ref{sec:ablation}) confirms that LP compression persists without constrained decoding; on RE, the interaction is task-dependent.
Diversity-stratified analysis confirms the gap persists even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}); RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339, preliminary; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}) may compound this.

\paragraph{The gap widens with $N$.}
Doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$ expands oracle headroom from 12.5 to 16.9~pp ($+4.4$~pp), yet signal-based selection fails to capture this growth.
LP, the best signal, improves by only $+0.4$~pp ($\Delta$: $+0.0{\to}+0.5$~pp), leaving 16.4~pp of headroom unrealized---a 31\% expansion of the gap.
VC deteriorates further ($\Delta$: $-2.5{\to}{-}3.1$~pp), a counterintuitive result for majority voting: with more candidates, systematic errors in entity-level frequency counts dominate, amplifying selection bias rather than correcting it.
On RE at $N{=}16$ (3-seed), the pattern is even more severe: oracle headroom reaches 17.1~pp, yet all four consistency signals fall below greedy (best: VC $\Delta{=}{-}0.8$~pp; worst: EM $\Delta{=}{-}1.5$~pp; all Fisher $p{>}0.77$; Table~\ref{tab:re_n16_selection}).
LP is the sole exception ($\Delta{=}{+}0.7$~pp, Fisher $p{=}0.058$), the only positive selection delta on either task at $N{=}16$, but does not reach significance.
This scaling behavior confirms that the correlation-selection gap is not a small-$N$ artifact; unsupervised signals face a structural ceiling that widens as oracle headroom grows.

\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here because the utility functions correlate with F1 at the instance level but not within a single instance---the mathematical essence of the correlation-selection gap.
\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs---consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.

\paragraph{Score compression under free-form decoding.}\label{sec:ablation}
A natural hypothesis is that LP compression is an artifact of constrained decoding's restricted token space.
We test this via controlled ablation on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, single dataset): generating free-form (unconstrained) outputs on the same instances with post-hoc JSON parsing (parse rate 99.95\%, 4406/4408; Table~\ref{tab:freeform_ablation}).
For NER, LP variance is essentially unchanged (within-instance std ratio $0.97{\times}$, tied fraction 59.7\%$\to$57.7\%) and selection gains remain negligible ($+0.18$~pp free-form vs.\ $+0.59$~pp constrained), establishing that NER LP compression persists independent of decoding regime in our setting.
However, the ablation reveals a task-dependent interaction: RE LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single seed).
This reversal falls within the NER bootstrap 95\% CI [$-3.0$, $+4.2$]~pp and is based on a single seed, so we do not treat it as a confirmed finding; it suggests that constrained decoding may interact differently with RE but requires multi-seed replication.
The NER/RE divergence indicates that the relationship between decoding regime and selection is task-specific in our setting.
Notably, the fine-tuned model achieved 99.95\% parse rate without grammar constraints, suggesting that constrained decoding's format-compliance role may be redundant for sufficiently fine-tuned models.

\paragraph{Task-specific decoding interactions.}
The free-form ablation reveals divergent behavior across tasks.
On RE, LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single RE benchmark), a reversal that spans all 7 relation types and is driven by selective variance reallocation ($p{<}0.0001$).
The win/loss ratio shifts from 36:59 (constrained) to 45:45 (free-form), with the gains concentrated on relation-dense instances (mean 3.3 gold relations).
This interaction does not generalize to NER, where selection remains negligible under both regimes.
This ablation uses a single seed (seed${=}42$); whether the RE reversal replicates across seeds and generalizes to other RE benchmarks warrants further investigation.
Second, the non-tied subset ($n{=}210$) is partially reshuffled under free-form decoding: Jaccard similarity between the constrained and free-form non-tied sets is 0.472, indicating that 87 instances newly gain LP discrimination while others lose it, yielding a $3{\times}$ increase in within-instance LP range for the newly non-tied subset.
Despite this reshuffling, aggregate NER selection gains remain negligible---score compression is not a fixed property of specific instances but rather a pervasive regime that shifts across instances without producing net selection improvement.
Free-form decoding also slightly improves quality estimation (NER VC $\rho$: 0.379$\to$0.409), though this does not translate to selection gains.

\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
The decoupling of quality estimation ($\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1) means evaluating on a single metric risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.
Effective selection likely requires per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}; $N$-scaling analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}) shows $N{=}8$ captures most quality estimation benefit.
Cross-dataset evaluation confirms that structural signals are robust to domain shift when the training schema subsumes the target (VC $\rho{=}0.469$ OOD vs.\ $0.379$ in-domain); the reverse direction fails due to catastrophic model failure, not signal failure (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).
Our findings are established under constrained decoding at 8B scale; a single-dataset NER ablation suggests LP compression persists without constrained decoding, but RE shows task-dependent interaction with decoding regime.
Whether these patterns generalize across datasets, model scales, and decoding strategies warrants further investigation.

132	\paragraph{Seed variability.}

136	The seed sensitivity underscores that single-seed selection evaluations---common in the literature---may overstate or understate signal utility by several percentage points, motivating our multi-seed design.
137	
138	\paragraph{Quality estimation $\neq$ output selection.}
139	Instance-level confidence signals predict \textit{which inputs} the model handles reliably, not \textit{which output} among $N$ candidates is best.
140	When per-sample variance is low relative to instance-level difficulty, even perfect quality estimation cannot discriminate among near-identical candidates.
141	This gap has direct consequences for test-time scaling in IE \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2025scaling}: closing it likely requires per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers}.

148	On RE, only VC consistently outperforms LP ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.012$, preliminary).
149	NER signals are reasonably calibrated (ECE 0.069--0.096; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}), while RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339) and compound errors impose a ceiling at $\rho{\approx}0.28$ for $N{=}16$.

1	\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}
2	
3	We systematically evaluate five confidence signals across quality estimation, binary discrimination, and sample selection for LLM-based structured IE, revealing that these metrics decouple---single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.
4	All signals achieve strong quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38, AUROC up to 0.75) yet none significantly improves sample selection on SciERC despite 12--18~pp oracle headroom---the \textit{correlation-selection gap}.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Self-consistency---sampling multiple outputs and aggregating them---has become a powerful strategy for improving language model reasoning.
On discrete-answer tasks such as arithmetic and commonsense QA, majority voting over chain-of-thought samples yields large gains: +18 percentage points on GSM8K (PaLM-540B; \citealp{wang2023selfconsistency}).
More broadly, test-time compute scaling through repeated sampling and selection has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling, offering substantial quality improvements at inference time \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
These results rest on a shared assumption: that among $N$ stochastic samples, a selection mechanism can identify better outputs.
For tasks with a single correct answer, this assumption holds naturally---the majority vote is the selector.
But information extraction (IE) poses a structurally different challenge.
The output is not a single token or number; it is a \textit{set} of entities or relations with internal dependencies, where two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical structures.
There is no obvious majority to vote on, partial agreement is the norm rather than the exception, and the space of valid outputs is combinatorially large.
Can self-consistency still provide useful signal in this structured setting?

Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated two distinct objectives: \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) and \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
These require different signal properties: the former benefits from instance-level aggregation, while the latter demands per-sample discrimination.
Self-consistency methods for discrete answers \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc} and weighted variants \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence---an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
The most relevant study, \citet{nedellec2026consistency}, examines consistency--accuracy correlations for LLM-based IE, finding results that our quality-estimation analysis corroborates.
Our work complements theirs in three directions: (i)~structural matching beyond surface-level agreement, (ii)~testing whether quality estimation translates to best-of-$N$ selection (it does not), and (iii)~a difficulty gradient revealing non-obvious findings---WNUT-17 conditional correlations collapse to $\rho{=}0.038$ (n.s.) and LP exhibits strong \textit{negative} correlation ($\rho{=}{-}0.410$)---that would be invisible on a single dataset.

Structured IE requires schema-compliant output, making constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided} the standard inference strategy---without it, a substantial fraction of outputs from general-purpose models are unparseable.\footnote{Fine-tuned models may retain format compliance without grammar constraints: our free-form ablation achieves 99.95\% valid JSON rate (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).}
All experiments use constrained decoding, the regime under which structured IE is practically deployed.

\caption{The correlation-selection gap. \textbf{Left}: high inter-sample agreement correlates with high F1 (quality estimation). \textbf{Right}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all candidates, precluding sample selection.}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Multi-metric evaluation revealing metric dissociation.}

    The empirical contribution is diagnosing why the two per-sample mechanisms that \textit{could} bridge the gap both fail: log-probability scores are compressed into effective ties (60\% of instances within $\varepsilon{=}0.05$), and consensus-proximity selection (MBR decoding) correlates with quality across instances but not within them.
    Where compression is mitigated, LP becomes a significant selector ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$), confirming score compression as the primary bottleneck.
    A controlled ablation confirms LP compression persists without constrained decoding on NER; on RE, LP selection reverses direction (preliminary), indicating task-dependent interaction with decoding regime.

    \item \textbf{Task-complexity boundary conditions.}
    Signal rankings shift with task difficulty: EM leads on easy tasks, SJ on hard tasks---consistent across two model families at 8B scale, though with model-dependent magnitude.
